exemplars.name: Java Memory Model
exemplars.question: What is the Java Memory Model and what does happens-before mean?

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand why multi-threaded Java programs can see stale data and how volatile, synchronized, and final establish visibility guarantees
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking that writing a value on one thread immediately makes it visible to all other threads — without synchronization the JVM and CPU can reorder operations and keep values in CPU registers or L1 cache
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Name specific happens-before rules (monitor unlock → lock, volatile write → read, thread start → first action), explain the double-checked locking bug and why volatile fixes it, and mention that the JMM is what makes all the Java concurrency utilities (CountDownLatch, BlockingQueue) safe

sections.title: The Problem: CPUs and JVMs Reorder Things
sections.content:
Modern CPUs don't execute instructions in program order — they reorder reads and writes to fill execution pipelines and keep the CPU busy. Each core has its own **L1/L2 cache**, meaning a value written by Core 1 might sit in Core 1's cache for an indefinite time before being flushed to main memory where Core 2 can see it.

The JVM adds another layer of reordering through **JIT compilation** — the Just-In-Time compiler rearranges bytecode for optimization, including hoisting reads out of loops and eliminating redundant stores. In a single-threaded program, both CPU and JIT reordering are invisible because they preserve the illusion of sequential execution. But in a **multi-threaded program**, Thread B can read a value that Thread A 'already wrote' — because A's write is still in A's L1 cache, or the JIT hoisted B's read above the point where A's write became visible.

The **JMM (Java Memory Model)** is the formal contract that specifies exactly which synchronization actions force writes to be flushed from caches and prevent the JIT from reordering across those boundaries. Without understanding the JMM, concurrent bugs appear to be non-deterministic — they work on your machine, fail in production, and disappear when you add debug logging (because `println` internally uses `synchronized`).

sections.title: volatile, synchronized, and the double-checked locking pattern
The Core Happens-Before Rules
sections.content:
- **Why JMM exists** — CPUs reorder reads/writes and cache values in L1. Without synchronization, `boolean running = false;` set by Thread A may never be seen by Thread B which loops on `while(running){}` forever
- **Happens-before = visibility guarantee** — if A happens-before B, all of A's writes are visible to B. It's about memory visibility, not wall-clock time
- **Three rules you must know**: (1) `synchronized` unlock → lock flushes all writes, (2) `volatile` write → read always sees latest value, (3) `Thread.start()` → child thread sees everything parent wrote before `start()`
- **Double-checked locking bug** — `instance = new Singleton()` involves multiple writes; without `volatile`, another thread sees a non-null reference to a half-constructed object. Fix: add `volatile` or use holder pattern
- **In practice** — use `java.util.concurrent` (ConcurrentHashMap, CompletableFuture, CountDownLatch) which are built on JMM guarantees internally; rarely need raw `synchronized` or `volatile`

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
The **Java Memory Model** defines when a write by one thread becomes visible to a read by another thread. The simplest example: Thread A sets `running = false`, but Thread B keeps looping on `while(running)` forever — because the JVM cached `running` in a CPU register and never re-read from main memory. Without synchronization, this is perfectly legal behavior.

The JMM solves this with the **happens-before** relationship. It's a visibility guarantee — if action A happens-before B, all of A's writes are visible to B. The three rules that matter most: first, a `synchronized` unlock happens-before the next lock on the same monitor, so everything the unlocking thread wrote is flushed. Second, a `volatile` write happens-before every subsequent read of that field — adding `volatile boolean running` fixes the example above. Third, `Thread.start()` happens-before the child thread's first action.

The classic interview example is **double-checked locking**. You write `if (instance == null) { synchronized(lock) { instance = new Singleton(); } }` — but `new Singleton()` involves multiple writes (allocate, initialize fields, assign reference). Without `volatile`, another thread can see a non-null `instance` pointing to a half-initialized object. Making the field `volatile` adds a happens-before edge that prevents this partial visibility. The cleaner alternative is the **holder pattern** — `private static class Holder { static final Singleton INSTANCE = new Singleton(); }` — which leverages the JVM's class-loading guarantees.

In practice, I rarely use raw `synchronized` or `volatile`. I rely on `java.util.concurrent` — `ConcurrentHashMap`, `CompletableFuture`, `CountDownLatch` — which are built on JMM guarantees internally. But understanding happens-before is essential when debugging production data races, like a missing `volatile` on a config flag causing stale reads for hours.

exemplars.name: Garbage Collection
exemplars.question: How does Java garbage collection work?

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand object lifecycle, what keeps an object alive, and how the JVM avoids scanning the whole heap on every GC cycle
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing 'garbage collected' with 'immediately freed' — GC is non-deterministic, and calling System.gc() is only a hint. Also confusing Young GC (minor) and Full GC (major) costs.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Name concrete collectors (G1GC, ZGC, Shenandoah), explain stop-the-world pauses, describe the remembered set / card table used to track old-to-young references, and mention GC tuning flags like -Xmx, -Xms, -XX:+UseG1GC

sections.title: What GC Does in One Sentence
sections.content:
In languages like C/C++, the programmer must manually allocate and free memory — forget to free, and you have a memory leak; free too early, and you have a dangling pointer crash. Java's **garbage collector** eliminates both problems by automatically reclaiming heap memory occupied by objects that no live thread can reach.

However, GC is not magic. It introduces **pauses** (stop-the-world events where application threads are frozen), and it can only collect truly **unreachable** objects — if your code accidentally keeps a reference to an object, GC considers it live. Understanding how GC works is essential for diagnosing performance issues (long pauses, high allocation rates) and memory leaks (objects that should be collectable but aren't).

sections.title: Phase 1 — Mark: tracing from GC roots
sections.content:
The GC doesn't scan the entire heap randomly — it starts from a specific set of **GC roots**, which are references that are guaranteed to be alive:
- **Stack variables** — every local variable and method parameter on every thread's call stack
- **Static fields** — fields declared `static` in loaded classes
- **JNI references** — objects held by native code via JNI
- **JVM internal** — classloaders, Thread objects, system classloader references

Starting from each root, the GC traverses every reference field recursively (like a graph traversal), marking each reachable object as **live**. Any object not reached by this traversal is **unreachable** — it's garbage and safe to reclaim. This is why Java doesn't have the circular-reference problem that plagues reference-counting schemes: if two objects reference each other but neither is reachable from any GC root, both are collected.

sections.title: Phase 2 — Sweep / Compact: reclaiming memory
sections.content:
After marking, the collector walks the heap and does one of:
- **Sweep** — records the locations of dead objects as free space (fast but causes fragmentation).
- **Compact** — moves live objects together and updates all references (eliminates fragmentation but requires stopping all threads — stop-the-world pause).
- **Copy** — copies live objects to a fresh memory region and discards the old region wholesale (used in Young generation; fast because most objects are dead).

sections.title: Phase 3 — Generational hypothesis: Young vs Old
sections.content:
The JVM heap is divided based on the observation that 'most objects die young':

- **Young generation** (Eden + two Survivor spaces): new objects are allocated in Eden. Minor GC runs frequently, copies live survivors to a Survivor space, and promotes long-lived objects to Old after a threshold number of minor GCs. Minor GC pauses are short (< 10 ms for G1GC).
- **Old generation** (Tenured): long-lived objects. Collected by major/mixed GC which scans more of the heap; pauses are longer.
- **Metaspace** (Java 8+, not PermGen): class metadata. Grows dynamically, limited by native memory.

To track references from Old → Young without scanning the entire Old generation on every minor GC, G1GC maintains a **remembered set** (per region) and a **card table** (dirty-bit array tracking modified old-gen regions).

sections.title: Memory leak patterns and GC-friendly code
Key Points
sections.content:
- **Reachability-based**, not reference counting — GC traces from roots (stack variables, static fields, JNI refs) and marks everything reachable. Circular references like `A→B→A` get collected if neither is reachable from a root
- **Generational heap** — Young gen (Eden + 2 Survivor spaces) collects frequently with minor GC (typically < 10ms); Old gen collects via major/mixed GC (longer pauses). Most objects die in Eden — ~95% are garbage after one minor GC
- **G1GC** (default since Java 9) divides heap into regions, collects "garbage-first" regions with most dead objects. Tune with `-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=200`. **ZGC** keeps pauses under 1ms even on 100GB+ heaps
- **Memory leaks = reference leaks** — a `static Map<String, byte[]>` that grows without eviction, an unclosed `InputStream`, or a registered listener never removed. These keep objects reachable, so GC can't touch them
- **Diagnostic toolkit**: GC logs (`-Xlog:gc*`), heap dumps analyzed with Eclipse MAT, `jmap -histo` for quick object counts, and Java Flight Recorder for runtime profiling

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Java GC is **reachability-based**, not reference-counted. The collector starts from **GC roots** — stack variables, static fields, JNI references — and traces every reference chain. Everything reachable is alive; everything else is garbage. This means circular references like `A→B→A` are collected perfectly fine, as long as neither is reachable from a root.

The heap is split into **generations** based on the observation that most objects die young. The **Young generation** (Eden + two Survivor spaces) is where new objects are allocated. A **minor GC** runs frequently, typically pausing for under 10ms, and reclaims ~95% of objects in Eden because they're already dead. Objects that survive enough minor GC cycles get **promoted** to the Old generation, which is collected less frequently with longer pauses.

**G1GC** is the default since Java 9. It divides the heap into fixed-size regions and collects the regions with the most garbage first — hence the name. You tune it with `-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=200` and let the collector decide how many regions to collect per cycle. **ZGC** (production-ready since Java 15) goes further — sub-millisecond pauses even on 100GB+ heaps, using colored pointers and load barriers.

The most important thing to understand about **memory leaks** in Java is that they're really **reference leaks**. A `static Map<String, byte[]>` that grows without eviction, an unclosed `InputStream`, a listener registered but never removed — these keep objects reachable, so the GC can't touch them. I diagnose them with GC logs (`-Xlog:gc*`), heap dumps analyzed in Eclipse MAT, and `jmap -histo` for quick object counts.
